resources.string: Watching traffic and applying your rules.
Nothing is being inspected or blocked.
This app\'s traffic goes straight out, exactly as if the firewall were off. Nothing about it is filtered, blocked or logged.
No rules apply to this app while it is skipping the firewall, and its connections will not appear in the traffic log.
This is your messaging app. Picture messages often travel on a separate carrier connection that the firewall cannot carry, so skipping the firewall here is the usual fix for MMS.
Send this app\'s connections through the Tor network using Orbot, so the sites it talks to see a Tor exit address instead of yours.
Requires Orbot, the Tor Project\'s app. Expect it to be slower, and expect some services to challenge or refuse traffic arriving from Tor.

Worth knowing: this hides your address from the sites this app reaches, but it is not anonymity. Your phone still looks up names normally, so your network provider can still see which sites you visit, and the app itself can still identify you by signing in. Connections that Tor cannot carry — anything over UDP, including video calls and QUIC — are dropped rather than sent unprotected.
Orbot is running and accepting connections.
Orbot is installed but not answering, so this app has no network at all right now. Start Orbot and check again.
Orbot is not installed, so nothing can be routed and this app has no network at all right now.
No connections yet. Open an app and traffic will show up here.
Start the firewall to see what your apps are connecting to.
Deny every app that you have not explicitly allowed. Expect things to break until you allow what you use.

Android encrypts DNS by default, which hides lookups from this app and stops domain rules working. This refuses DNS-over-TLS so lookups fall back to a form that can be filtered. Ignored if you set a specific Private DNS server.
Drop IPv6 so apps fall back to IPv4. Useful if you want every connection to show up under one address family.
Bring the firewall back up after a restart, as long as VPN permission is still granted.
How far to go after the services that profile you across apps and sites.
No tracker lists. Ad and malware lists are unaffected.
Blocks analytics and phone-maker telemetry — the kind apps send and never read a reply to. Shopping and referral links stay working. This should not break anything.
Also blocks attribution, measurement and consent services. Some apps wait on these before they will load, so expect to allow the occasional domain by hand.
Keeps list downloads off your mobile data allowance.
Lists are maintained by third parties and can occasionally block something you want. Add the domain to the allowed list below to override any of them.
One per line. Blocking example.com also blocks anything under it, such as ads.example.com.
Exceptions that win over the blocklist. Use these to punch a hole in a broad entry.
Removes every per-app rule and both domain lists. The IPv6 setting is kept.
This clears all of your app rules and domain lists. It cannot be undone.
Domain rules work by watching plain DNS. Apps that use DNS over HTTPS or hard-coded IP addresses will bypass them, so per-app rules are the reliable layer.
Shows that the firewall tunnel is running.
